articles.abstract: Norms are fundamental to social life, but basic questions about how they are affected by social context remain. Specifically, how do normative constraints depend on the presence and status of observers, and how do such relational contingencies vary across cultures? Using data from more than 25,000 individuals across 90 societies, we test several hypotheses linking normative constraints on everyday behaviors (like arguing, laughing, cursing, kissing, and crying), to the presence and status of observers. We find that behaviors widely viewed as appropriate in private become more constrained in the presence of others (an observer effect), and even more so when those others are higher in status (a status effect). Both observer and status effects are culturally universal, but the observer effect shows more variation across cultures. In particular, we find that observer effects are larger in societies that emphasize individualizing moral foundations, that is, avoiding harm and unfairness to others, because these societies are more permissive of actions when others are not around. The relative stability of status effects across cultural contexts suggests a universal tendency to defer in social hierarchies. These findings shed light on the relational contingency of everyday norms and underscore the role of such norms in the maintenance of social order and reproduction of inequality.

articles.title: Revealed Social Networks
articles.authors: Christopher P Chambers, Yusufcan Masatlioglu, Christopher Turansick
articles.abstract: The linear-in-means model is the standard empirical model of peer effects and asks that an agent’s choice or outcome is a combination of their ideal point and the mean outcome of their group. Using choice data and exogenous group variation, we develop a revealed preference style test for the linear-in-means model. This test is formulated as a linear program and can be interpreted as a condition about differentiating the behaviour of each agent in a consistent manner. We then study the identification properties of the linear-in-means model. A key takeaway from our analysis is the close relationship between the dimension of the outcome variable and identification. When the outcome variable is one-dimensional, failures of identification are generic. When the outcome variable is multidimensional, we provide natural conditions under which identification is generic.

articles.title: Beyond Informality: How Chinese Migrants Transformed a Border Economy. By DouglasdeToledo Piza, Stanford, CA: Stanford University Press, 2025. 234 pp. $28.00 (ebook). ISBN: 978‐1‐50‐364332‐1
Care Preferences Beyond Filial Piety: How Second‐Generation Chinese Migrants in the Netherlands Plan Care for Ageing Parents?
articles.abstract: As more first‐generation Chinese migrants in the Netherlands reach older age, increased attention is required to reconcile their care needs and expectations with the expectations and perspectives of their adult children. Moving beyond filial piety, this study examines how second‐generation Chinese migrants develop and reflect on their preferences and plans for their parents' care. The study employs a developmental life course perspective (DLCP) to contribute to the understanding of the evolution of care planning from an individual perspective. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews, the findings show that adult children are generally willing to support their parents, but seek simultaneously to establish boundaries in response to parental expectations. Institutional care is often preferred over family‐based care, particularly when intensive support is anticipated. In this regard, filial piety is neither fully nor seamlessly transmitted across generations. The analysis based on DLCP sheds light on multiple tensions that are either intensified or mitigated through the perceived relevance of Dutch and Chinese cultures, past and present parent–child relationships, sibling dynamics, and agency in striving toward ideal care arrangements.

articles.title: ‘People Recognise Us as the Bravest of the Brave’: Retired Gurkha Soldiers Negotiating Employment, Racialisation and Identity in Britain
articles.abstract: This article aims to contribute new insights into ageing migrants and masculinity by drawing upon life story interviews with retired Nepali Gurkha soldiers settled in South‐East England. Less is known about middle‐aged and older migrants who migrate not to retire per se but to pursue a second or third career in later life. Our research adds new insights into how these men mobilise capitals to navigate new and unfamiliar job markets, post‐retirement, in their middle and older age. Drawing upon the concept of ‘presentation of self’, the paper illustrates how Gurkha men utilise their martial identity—as brave, strong and loyal ex‐soldiers in the British Army—to challenge discrimination and navigate new lives in Britain. However, the Gurkha image is also based on colonial racialisation. Nonetheless, we find that preserving their Gurkha identity and their legacy of service to the British Crown was not only to gain recognition of their military service and unique status, but also to assert their masculine identities in the new contexts in Britain.

articles.title: Rank, Degrading Treatment, and the Italy‐Albania Agreement
articles.abstract: In November 2023, Italy signed a five‐year agreement with Albania to transfer asylum seekers intercepted in international waters by Italian vessels to Italian‐run detention centres in Albania for asylum processing and deportation. The agreement has been controversial and raises several human rights issues. This article examines these human rights concerns and argues that the agreement is degrading by design. Analysing policy documents, legal cases, speeches, international human rights and refugee law, and philosophical and legal scholarship on the concept of degrading treatment, this article argues that the cumulative effect of subjecting people to unnecessary suffering, discrimination, and dehumanisation creates a structural risk of degrading human dignity that brings asylum seekers down in rank. This article makes an important contribution to the policy debates over the externalisation of asylum seekers in Europe by shedding light on the link between policy designs and the risk of degrading treatment.

Whataboutism in International Diplomacy: Shaping Third-Party Public Attitudes Toward U.S. Foreign Policy
articles.authors: Wilfred M. Chow, Dov H. Levin, Atsushi Tago
articles.abstract: How does whataboutism influence the attitudes of third-party and allied audiences during international diplomatic exchanges? States openly accused of misconduct often employ whataboutism, deflecting criticism by highlighting the accuser’s own transgressions. Although policymakers frequently discuss whataboutism, research on its effects—especially on third-party publics—is limited. This study addresses the gap by examining via survey experiments a “hard case”: the impact of whataboutism targeting the U.S. on Japanese and the British publics, two steadfast U.S. allies. Our findings reveal that whataboutism significantly undermines support for the critic’s actions and diminishes the willingness of these populations to back sanctions led by the critic against states engaging in whataboutism. These results, the first empirical evidence of whataboutism’s effects on third-party allied publics, highlight whataboutism’s potency in shaping international public opinion, even among audiences from nations closely aligned with the critic country, potentially constraining U.S. foreign policy options.

articles.title: From state heroes to social pariahs? Civilian hiring and voluntary service in Russia’s war in Ukraine
articles.abstract: Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has produced a politically charged cohort of veterans whom the state publicly celebrates as heroes. Yet in a context where even the word “war” can be criminalised, how civilians actually regard different categories of service is difficult to observe through conventional measures. This research note uses labour-market behaviour as a window into those politically sensitive distinctions. Combining a correspondence audit—a standard tool in discrimination research—with a Bayesian sequential design that learns efficiently under real-world constraints, I sent 60 matched pairs of fictitious résumés to vacancies on major Russian job platforms in 2025. Within each pair, one applicant signalled voluntary contract service in the war, the other only routine conscription. Applicants foregrounding voluntary service received roughly a third fewer callbacks (Δ=0.18, 95% credible interval above zero), with consistent results across Bayesian and frequentist specifications. The design cannot identify the mechanism behind this penalty—employers may be reacting to perceived trauma, discipline concerns, reputational risk, or quieter political distancing from the war. But the finding is clear: in this platform-based segment of Russia’s civilian labour market, signalling voluntary participation in the war reduced employer interest rather than enhancing it. If the state’s heroic narrative translated straightforwardly into civilian life, the opposite should hold.

articles.title: Purging the police in nascent democracies
articles.abstract: How do new democracies reckon with inherited authoritarian enforcement agencies? Obviously, they can disband these agencies and build new ones (thorough purge) or make former agents work for the new regime (no purge). A third way is to purge selectively: evaluate each agent, case by case. We argue that, even accounting for self-selection, such selective purges are most likely to succeed when agents are moderate in competence and ideology. When the pool of agents is less competent or more loyal to the ancien regime, selective purges give way to thorough purges; when competence and loyalty are high, “no purges” are preferred. This theory is supported with data on the operation of vetting commissions in 49 sub-national regions of Poland. We analyze these data after developing a systematic approach to case selection that builds on the Most Similar Systems Design method, traditionally used for theory building.

articles.title: Prior government experience of rebel leaders and civil war duration
articles.abstract: Why does conflict termination occur during some rebel leaders’ tenures but not others? Under similar structural and organizational conditions, can rebel leadership help explain this variation? Although recent research has increasingly examined the role of rebel leaders, explanations of civil war duration have more often emphasized conflict-level and organizational conditions. This study builds on the emerging leader-level perspective by examining whether rebel leaders’ prior government experience affects the likelihood of conflict termination during their tenure. It argues that leaders with this experience may have capabilities that shorten conflict. Prior government experience can give future rebel leaders direct familiarity with state institutions and high-level political decision-making. This experience may help them build more effective rebel organizations and better assess opportunities for conflict termination once war begins. The argument is tested with data from the ROLE and UCDP Conflict Termination datasets for the period 1980–2011. Using Cox proportional hazards models, the study analyses the duration of civil war under individual rebel leaders. The results provide strong and consistent evidence that prior government experience significantly increases the likelihood of conflict termination during a leader’s tenure. Additional analyses are consistent with the article’s capability framework, showing that government experience is associated with stronger rebel organizational development and wartime performance. These results underscore the importance of distinguishing among leadership backgrounds and suggest that prior government experience can significantly shape civil war duration.

articles.title: Interactive representations of power and status signals in learning social hierarchies
articles.authors: Chunliang Feng, Feilong Liu, Binjie Yang, Edmund Derrington, Yuejia Luo, Chen Qu, Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Social hierarchies, which organize our social relationships, have heterogeneous effects on choice behavior. Two central dimensions of social hierarchies, status, which is earned through recognition of competence, and power, which is the capacity to control the outcomes of others, may contribute to different behavioral profiles. Yet, the neurocomputational processes by which status- and power-related signals are learned based on social feedback, and influence subsequent decision-making, remain unclear. Here, we combine functional neuroimaging with computational modeling to examine how individuals acquire knowledge about others’ status and power, and how these learned hierarchy signals shape social influence on advice-taking during a risky choice task. We found that the medial prefrontal cortex covaried with status estimates, whereas the amygdala covaried with power estimates. Moreover, estimates in one dimension influenced choices in the other during learning. This indicates interactions between status and power signals, with retrosplenial cortex activity associated with hierarchy signals beyond immediate choice demands. Finally, status broadly modulated response biases toward both safe and risky advice, whereas power primarily increased bias toward safe advice. These findings characterize how experimentally instantiated status and power signals are learned and influence risky decision-making, indicating partially separable yet interactive representations of these hierarchy signals.

articles.title: Perfectibility in science and democracy: Institutions that learn
Indirect reciprocity with dual private assessment
articles.authors: Yukari Jessica Tham, Christian Hilbe, Yohsuke Murase
articles.abstract: People often cooperate out of concern for their reputation. The corresponding theory of indirect reciprocity predicts that such cooperation can only evolve if people’s opinions of each other are sufficiently correlated. This correlation, however, can be difficult to achieve when individuals form their opinions independently from one another, as in private assessment models. In that case, errors can generate disagreements that propagate throughout a population. Here, we identify a simple mechanism that mitigates this problem. Most prior work assumes that observers revise only the reputations of donors—the individuals who choose whether to cooperate or defect. We instead allow observers to also revise the reputations of recipients—the individuals affected by the donors’ choices. Using analytical calculations and simulations, we show that such dual reputation updates help synchronize opinions and facilitate cooperation. To demonstrate this approach, we focus on a particularly simple rule, which we call Recipient Image Scoring (RIS). Under RIS, recipients are assessed as good whenever donors choose to cooperate with them. We show that this rule for judging recipients effectively complements the classical leading-eight rules for judging donors. Our results establish dual assessment as a simple mechanism for cooperation that relies only on directly observable information.

articles.title: Face‐to‐Face With Administrative Burdens: Design Simplification, Emotional Costs, and Procedural Outcomes in Digital Welfare Applications
articles.authors: Fabian Hattke, Judith Hattke, David Hensel, Pamela Herd, Janne Kalucza, Donald Moynihan, Rick Vogel
articles.abstract: Recent scholarship on administrative burden has increasingly focused on psychological costs, design interventions, and digital burdens. This study combines these interests and examines the psychological costs of negative emotions during administrative encounters at varying levels of digital maturity. Building on affective events theory and employing facial coding in a controlled experiment, the study demonstrates that negative emotions rise during bureaucratic encounters, with frustration resulting in more errors made by applicants. Simplifying the procedure through pre‐filled forms does not reduce negative emotional arousal; however, it enhances satisfaction with the procedure. Vulnerable citizens, as indicated by low education and foreign citizenship, benefit more from this informational integration than other groups, suggesting that procedural redesign can enhance the inclusiveness of public service delivery. Overall, the research advances both scholarly and practical understanding of the emotional dimension of administrative burdens from a process‐oriented perspective, highlighting the persistent challenge of reducing emotional costs to enhance citizen experiences.

articles.title: Rethinking Top Public Management Through Relational Dynamics: A Systems‐Informed Study of Senior Executives
articles.authors: Ximena Pizarro‐Bore, Javier Fuenzalida, Norma M. Riccucci, Constanza Faune
articles.abstract: The complex nature of top public managerial work is widely acknowledged in theory but rarely examined empirically. Existing research has mostly analyzed bivariate relationships among core components of top managerial work in government, including managers' attributes, practices, outcomes, and contexts. Drawing on a systems‐based framework, we investigate how effective top managerial work unfolds as a complex relational practice. We analyze seven cases of long‐serving, distinguished Chilean senior executives through a comprehensive and process‐oriented lens, based on 27 semi‐structured interviews with the managers and members of their personal and professional networks. Our findings indicate how the relational dynamics in which senior public executives engage shape their managerial attributes and practices. Specifically, strategizing, motivation building, and technical expertise are best understood as emerging primarily through interactions within agencies and with external sociopolitical environments. These results qualify perspectives that explain senior public management effectiveness by overemphasizing executives' individual attributes and views, and underscore the need for personnel policies and governance environments that equip managers with the capacities called for by a systems approach to top public management.

articles.title: Does Gender Budgeting Improve Women's Well‐Being, Equality, and Empowerment?
articles.authors: Marjorie De la Cruz, Milena I. Neshkova, Yoon‐Jung Choi
articles.abstract: The United Nations' fifth Sustainable Development Goal calls for gender equality and empowerment. Gender budgeting (GB) has been proposed as a potential mechanism to reduce gender disparities. This is a novel approach to budgeting that considers the impact of public spending on women and other underrepresented groups. Despite its growing popularity, spreading to over 80 countries since its launch in the 1980s, the effectiveness of GB remains less understood. This study tests whether GB has led to tangible improvements in women's well‐being, equality, and empowerment. We use an event study research design with staggered adoption to analyze data across 47 countries from 2000 to 2023. Our analyses of average and heterogeneous treatment effects reveal short‐ and long‐term impacts; notably, we find significant reductions in maternal mortality ratios and adolescent birth rates, as well as improvements in women's political empowerment.

articles.title: Negotiating Presence: The Dynamics of Passive Representation Among Ultra‐Orthodox Women in Public Organizations
articles.abstract: Studies in representative bureaucracy have focused on whether passive representation translates into active representation. We shift this analytical lens by conceptualizing passive representation not as a static demographic condition or a preliminary stage, but as a dynamic organizational process. Drawing on 15 in‐depth interviews and a focus group with 14 ultra‐Orthodox women serving in mid‐ and senior‐level public positions in Israel, we examine how passive representation is enacted, negotiated, and gradually institutionalized in male‐dominated settings. Findings show how women's underrepresentation structures their entry and advancement through informal expectations and gendered networks, and how women “negotiate presence” by building legitimacy through heightened professionalism, creative networking in the face of gender segregation, and strategic engagement with supportive leaders. Through mentoring and gate‐opening practices, our participants created ripple effects that increased access for others over time. We argue that passive representation is a relational and evolving mechanism shaped by role interpretations and organizational constraints, reshaping access and participation even without formal policy changes.

articles.title: Sifting Through: Federal Separations in 2025 and Their Implications for Knowledge Loss and Agency Capacity
articles.authors: M. Blake Emidy, Anmol Soni, Evan Mistur
articles.abstract: The federal service experienced unprecedented turnover in the first year of the second Trump administration. Early reports have documented the substantial losses of personnel and the politicization and antagonism underlying those changes. This research breaks down separations over the past year, with a focus on the Deferred Resignation Program (DRP), to understand where turnover occurred and how it affected organizational knowledge and capacity. The analysis examines federal workforce data from January 2015 to December 2025 and reveals that the federal service lost substantial expertise and experience through both voluntary and involuntary means of separation. These results shed light on the fallout from 2025 executive actions, clarify the implications for government capacity, and point out prospective pathways for mitigating damages to the federal service moving forward.

articles.title: Informal Authority, Legitimacy Transition, and Institutional Change: A Theory of Advisory Capture
articles.abstract: How do informal actors achieve rapid bureaucratic dismantlement without formal authority? Analyzing the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) initiative, this article argues that when performance‐based legitimacy displaces procedural legitimacy as the dominant evaluative framework, informal actors can bypass established safeguards and reshape government institutions. Three concepts capture this process: advisory capture , legitimacy regime transition , and constrained coercion . The analysis reveals that dismantlement targets agencies based on political vulnerability rather than functional logic, that informal authority becomes institutionalized through formal rulemaking such as the Schedule Policy/Career rule, and that judicial review operates as ongoing contestation rather than definitive constraint. Protecting democratic governance requires defending not only formal rules but the legitimacy regimes within which those rules derive meaning.

articles.title: Tax Mobilization in Africa: Is the Secret Hidden in Women's Political Empowerment?
articles.authors: Gaston Brice Nkoumou Ngoa, Donald Ferdinand Okere Atanga, Marie Laure Belomo Onguene
articles.abstract: This article examines the effects of women's political empowerment (WPE) on tax revenue mobilization using a panel sample of 41 African countries over the 2000–2022 period. Utilizing the system Generalized Method of Moments, the empirical results demonstrate that WPE significantly enhances tax revenue mobilization in Africa. This finding remains robust to alternative measures of both WPE and tax revenue. Furthermore, beyond a specific turning point, increased WPE tends to diminish tax revenue mobilization. Finally, the study highlights that WPE operates through several transmission channels, including corruption control, the size of the informal economy, and female labor force participation. In terms of public policy, strengthening gender quotas within the African political sphere is crucial to enhancing tax mobilization. Nonetheless, given the threshold effects identified in this relationship, policymakers must prioritize the quality of women's political representation rather than focusing solely on increasing their numerical representation within political decision‐making circles.

Early-Career Discrimination: Spiraling or Self-Correcting?
articles.authors: Arjada Bardhi, Yingni Guo, Bruno Strulovici
articles.abstract: Do workers from social groups with comparable productivity distributions obtain comparable lifetime earnings? We study how a small amount of early-career discrimination propagates over time when workers’ productivity is revealed through employment. In breakdown learning environments that primarily track on-the-job failures, such discrimination spirals into a substantial lifetime earnings gap for groups of comparable productivity, whereas in breakthrough learning environments that track successes, early-career discrimination can be self-corrected, so comparable groups obtain comparable lifetime earnings. This contrast persists in large labor markets and with flexible wages, inconclusive learning, and misspecified employer beliefs.

articles.title: Affective Polarization, Media Outlets, and Opinion Dynamics
articles.authors: Sebastiano Della Lena, Luca Paolo Merlino, Yves Zenou
articles.abstract: We study opinion dynamics in a social network consisting of two groups. Agents update their opinions by conforming to members of their own group while rejecting the views of the opposing group (affective polarization), and by listening to a media outlet that may provide biased information. We characterize the long-run opinions and identify when affective polarization and media bias lead to ideological polarization, persistent disagreement, or failures of learning. We also derive when information interventions or censorship improve the accuracy of average opinions} and reduce disagreement, and when they backfire: better information helps only under specific media bias configurations and when directed to the agents we identify as most effective at propagating it through the network.

articles.title: Recruiting Talent
articles.authors: Simon Board, Moritz Meyer-ter-Vehn, Tomasz Sadzik
articles.abstract: We study a parsimonious model of a competitive labor market in which firms privately screen workers to identify talent. The equilibrium exhibits dispersion in wages and productivity; when talent is scarce, firms with superior screening skills post higher wages, attract better applicants, and recruit more talented workers. High-wage firms impose a compositional externality on low-wage firms, leading to equilibrium inefficiency: Welfare would be higher if low-skilled firms posted high wages and selected first. We also provide a micro-foundation for firms heterogeneous screening skills. When talented workers are better at screening (e.g. via superior referrals), a dynamic version of the economy converges to a unique steady state in which differences in talent, profits and screening skills persist forever.

articles.title: Labor Supply and the Pension Contribution-Benefit Link
articles.authors: Eric French, Attila Lindner, Cormac O’Dea, Tom Zawisza
articles.abstract: We estimate the impact of public pension incentives on labor supply far from the normal retirement age by exploiting Poland's switch from a Defined Benefit to a Notional Defined Contribution (NDC) scheme. This reform created a sharp cohort-based discontinuity in the link between current pension contributions and future benefits. Using this discontinuity and the universe of taxpayers, we estimate an employment elasticity with respect to the net return to work of 0.51 for men at ages 51-54. We estimate a lifecycle model to match these responses and discuss the broader implications of the reform. The shift to NDC reallocates work incentives over the lifecycle, strengthening incentives at younger ages, when labor supply is relatively inelastic, and weakening them at older ages, when labor supply is more elastic. This reallocation of work incentives tends to reduce aggregate lifecycle labor supply, which highlights the advantage of targeting pension incentives towards ages at which labor supply is most responsive.

articles.title: Why Veil? Religious Headscarves and the Economic Role of Women
articles.abstract: We show that the emergence of new economic opportunities that draw women away from their traditional domestic roles has significantly influenced the adoption of religious veiling. We measure the prevalence of veiling among young women across Indonesia’s districts for more than two decades by hand-coding around a quarter million photographs attached to Indonesia’s public high school registers. To establish causality, we exploit exogenous variation generated by international demand for Indonesia’s products, interacted with the gender and sectoral composition of local industries. Districts exposed to stronger positive economic shocks—and thus greater economic opportunities for women—exhibit higher rates of veiling adoption. Our findings suggest that veiling facilitates young women’s participation in formal labor markets while safeguarding their personal and social image in society.

articles.title: Paying to Match: Decentralized Markets with Information Frictions
articles.authors: Marina Agranov, Ahrash Dianat, Larry Samuelson, Leeat Yariv
articles.abstract: We experimentally study decentralized one-to-one matching markets with transfers. We vary the information available to participants, complete or incomplete, and the surplus structure, supermodular or submodular. Several insights emerge. First, while markets often culminate in efficient matchings, stability is more elusive, reflecting the difficulty of arranging attendant transfers. Second, incomplete information and submodularity present hurdles to efficiency and especially stability; their combination drastically diminishes stability's likelihood. Third, matchings form ``from the top down'' in complete-information supermodular markets, but exhibit many more and less-obviously ordered offers otherwise. Last, participants' market positions matter far more than their dynamic bargaining styles for outcomes.

articles.title: The worst energy policy in the world
articles.abstract: The Iran war could serve as a turning point in accelerating the global transition away from fossil fuels: Every additional day that oil and gas prices are high and future supplies are uncertain, wind and solar power—cheaper and more scalable than ever before—grow all the more appealing. But nearly half of the world’s countries have adopted emergency subsidies that research shows will make this transition slower, more expensive, and less equitable.

articles.title: Reproduction, rejection, or adoption of indigeneity? Intergenerational patterns of ethnic classification in contemporary Mexico
articles.abstract: This paper examines the intergenerational transmission of Indigenous classification in Mexico, focusing on how respondents reproduce, reject, or adopt Indigenous identification in relation to how they classify their parents. Drawing on data from a novel, nationally representative survey, I analyze factors associated with two key trajectories: de-indigenization, in which respondents who classify at least one parent as Indigenous do not self-classify as Indigenous, and indigenization, in which individuals who claim no Indigenous parentage come to identify as Indigenous. The findings show that roughly 16 percent of the population differs from how they report their parents’ Indigenous status. Reports of the loss of Indigenous language across generations are primarily associated with de-indigenization. In contrast, perceived phenotypical features commonly linked to Indigenous belonging and reports of Indigenous language proficiency are more strongly associated with indigenization. Additionally, a notable subset (10 percent) identifies as both Indigenous and mestizo, a classification path correlated with higher levels of education. These patterns reveal the fluidity of ethnoracial boundaries in Mexico and illustrate how processes of cultural transmission, racialization, and stratification shape the social production of Indigenous identity through different pathways.

articles.title: Sex differences in academic achievement in US adolescents: the role of maturation and impulse control
articles.abstract: This study investigates mechanisms underlying girls’ academic advantage over boys by examining the role of physical and pubertal maturation. Using longitudinal data from the Add Health study, we analyzed whether sex differences in maturation explain girls’ higher grade 10 GPAs, and whether these associations are mediated by planfulness or impulse control. Path analysis revealed that females’ higher GPAs were partially explained by their advanced physical maturation as rated by the interviewer (explaining 2.4 percent) and greater impulse control (explaining 7.7 percent), controlling for cognitive ability and other potential confounders. Still, a significant direct effect of biological sex on GPA remained, suggesting additional unexplained mechanisms. Planfulness predicted GPA but did not vary by sex, and neither planfulness nor impulse control were associated with perceived relative maturation.

articles.title: Beyond hiring: the dynamics of ethnic disparities in unemployment
articles.authors: Raffaele Grotti, Siddartha Aradhya, Juho Härkönen
articles.abstract: Many ethnic and racial minorities experience higher unemployment rates than majority populations. Recent research in this area has largely focused on inequalities in getting a job—through employer discrimination in hiring—using field experiments. While these studies typically identify significant levels of discrimination, they rarely examine or discuss how hiring discrimination contributes to ethnic employment penalties at the aggregate level. Our study draws attention to the role of ethnic and racial inequalities in getting a job but also in remaining employed and avoiding unemployment as factors contributing to aggregate ethnic employment penalties. Our analysis employs population register data from Sweden to estimate unemployment entry and exit rates for the majority and ten groups of children of immigrants (the second generation, G2). Based on counterfactual scenarios we conclude that the substantially higher unemployment rates among the G2 are driven by their higher risk of becoming unemployed rather than their lower chances of becoming employed. Our findings indicate that hiring discrimination and other reasons for inequalities in getting a job play a less significant role than sometimes assumed in explaining ethnic employment penalties—at least in the context of Sweden.

Childcare in Transition: Evidence That Patterns of Childcare Differ by Degree of Market Integration in Northwestern Tanzania
articles.authors: Anushé Hassan, David W. Lawson, Susan B. Schaffnit, Mark Urassa, Rebecca Sear
articles.abstract: Highlights This study uses novel data on multiple childcare types from both kin and nonkin in two culturally similar communities with varying market integration. It tests the hypothesis that market integration is associated with reduced kin support. Who provides support and the type of support vary by level of market integration. Market integration disrupts childcare support from paternal but not maternal kin. Distant kin and nonkin substitute for reduced support from close kin in the study's town.

Partisan bias in a sorted party system: A problem of epistemic inequality
articles.abstract: Normative and empirical scholars typically treat partisans’ distrust of their political rivals as a product of individual cognitive biases. But even if bias is inevitable, it is parties’ coalition‐building and messaging strategies that determine who bias is directed toward. This paper argues that the social sorting of party conflict exacerbates the epistemic and democratic harm of partisan distrust by generating distinctive patterns of epistemic inequality. I show that when voters associate parties with particular social groups, members of those groups suffer greater risk of testimonial injustice and related credibility deficits owing to their perceived partisanship. These dynamics are most damaging for members of marginalized groups, as party–group overlap can reinforce the prejudices they already face. Addressing these harms, I argue, requires looking beyond individual partisans to the background features of party systems that shape how elites mobilize group identities and animus in the struggle for office.

articles.title: From Exposure to Creation: Cultivating Narrative Ownership to Reduce Stigma
articles.abstract: Stories are powerful agents of attitude change, including attitudes toward stigmatized groups. However, existing theories have focused on narrative exposure, with limited attention to narrative creation. Creating a story involves simulating characters and events and expressing them through language, which may engage unique psychological processes. This research investigates how and why creating stories shapes stigma. In three experiments, participants wrote, imagined, or read a positive story about a stigmatized character. Study 1 showed that narrative creation, especially writing, increased psychological ownership, which predicted greater transportation and lower stigma. Study 2 replicated these findings using a different stigmatized group. Study 3 showed that psychological ownership continued to explain the effects of narrative creation above and beyond perceived agency. These findings extend theories of narrative persuasion by considering the effects of story creation on intergroup attitudes and introducing psychological ownership as a novel mechanism linking creation to narrative processing and outcomes.

articles.title: Less Effort to Believe and More Effort to Disbelieve: Examining the Interplay between News-Finds-Me and Affective Polarization in Political Fake News Susceptibility in the United States
articles.authors: Yu Tian, Lars Willnat, Baohua Zhou
articles.abstract: Drawing upon an online survey of 719 US adult partisans incorporating response latency data, we connected News-Finds-Me (NFM) to the partisan-motivated reasoning literature and theorized it as a consensus-based mode of news exposure that leads to different news-processing pathways, where the vested news-processing effort depends on whether the political falsehood aligns with one’s partisan identity and surrounding majority opinion. Individual-level analysis and headline-level modeling jointly illuminated the asymmetric interplay between NFM and affective polarization. In partisan-consistent scenarios, high-NFM users devoted limited processing time, falling short of cognitive effort to enable affect-laden, directional believing of partisan-consistent fake news. However, when challenged by partisan inconsistency, high-NFM users dedicated significantly more processing time, which exacerbated the relationship between affective polarization and refutation of partisan-inconsistent falsehoods. Contrarily, such an effort discrepancy, widely documented in the partisan-motivated reasoning literature, was weakened or reversed for low-NFM individuals. Extending the “Effort-Reinforces-Directional-Reasoning” thesis to fake news vulnerability, our findings underscore the paradoxical interplay between NFM and affective polarization: while NFM and affective polarization deviate people from active news-seeking and accuracy-oriented reasoning, their joint dynamics form a type of group thinking that reduces vulnerability to partisan falsehoods—even those aligned with one’s partisan attachments.

articles.title: Does disability trump family background? Determinants of electoral participation among young individuals with intellectual disability
articles.authors: Björn Boman, Jonas Hultin Rosenberg, Johan Wejryd
articles.abstract: Systematic differences of electoral participation between various social groups indicate crucial constraints of comprehensive democratic inclusion. Yet, there is a dearth of research on electoral participation among individuals with intellectual disability (ID), whose participation rates are considerably lower than among non‐ID citizens. This study examines determinants of electoral participation among individuals with ID based on administrative records covering five cohorts of individuals from the Swedish upper‐secondary school for pupils with ID ( N = 8438), and their parents. Our main results indicate that the severity of the disability and parents who have voted are the strongest predictors of voting among individuals with ID. The latter suggests that family background is vital. However, the socioeconomic status of the families, such as parents' level of education, income, and occupation, are less pivotal factors.

articles.title: Not‐so‐great expectations: Outgroup indifference facilitates conflict resolution in negatively interdependent contexts
articles.authors: Smadar Cohen‐Chen, Garrett L. Brady, Gerben A. van Kleef, Eran Halperin
articles.abstract: We examined how responses to outgroup indifference in conflict are shaped by the perceived nature of interdependence, which changes expectations of outgroup emotions toward the ingroup. Unlike conflicts perceived as positively interdependent, we hypothesized that in conflicts perceived as negatively interdependent, outgroup indifference would constitute a positive expectancy violation, thereby inviting favorable responses. Moreover, we examined affective and inferential processes as mediators across four studies ( N = 2521). In Study 1, outgroup indifference (vs. anger and hatred but not hope) reduced negative emotions (but did not affect expected collaboration), subsequently increasing support for cooperation. Study 2 added qualitative measures and showed that outgroup indifference (vs. anger) increased support for cooperation through decreased negative emotions and increased expected collaboration. Study 3 provided correlational evidence that perceptions of interdependence predict participants' expectations of outgroup emotions. Lastly, in Study 4, outgroup indifference increased expected collaboration and emotions when interdependence was perceived as negative.

articles.title: Diagnosing Institutional Design‐Implementation Gaps: A Dual‐Layer Systems Modeling Language Protocol for Visualizing Institutional Change Mechanisms
articles.authors: Sina Jangjoo, Tian Tang, Laura Arpan, Emily Lapan, D. G. Webster, Patrick Bitterman, John C. Little, Amro M. Farid
articles.abstract: This study introduces a dual‐layer protocol for diagnosing how formal institutional designs are implemented in practice in complex governance systems. The protocol builds two linked process maps; one for the formal rules and procedures (rules‐in‐form) and one for the routines actors actually follow in practice (rules‐in‐use). We adapt Systems Modeling Language (SysML), a graphical notation from systems engineering for specifying and analyzing complex socio‐technical systems, to represent both formal workflows and observed rules‐in‐use, and then overlay the two maps to identify divergence nodes where practice bypasses, supplements, or otherwise alters formally prescribed processes. Using Chesapeake Bay watershed governance as an illustrative case, the method shows how drift, layering, conversion, and displacement become visible through recurring divergences in data submission, model review, and approval routines, including socio‐technical artifacts such as data schemas, model parameters, and verification procedures. By producing transparent, empirically checkable visualizations linked to qualitative and documentary evidence, the protocol supports comparative institutional diagnostics and more targeted inquiry into where formal–informal gaps emerge and how they operate in collaborative governance. The study contributes to institutional analysis and policy process research by making visible the mechanisms through which gradual institutional change unfolds in collaborative governance and by offering a replicable way to represent implementation architecture and make socio‐technical dependencies more readily inspectable through an open systems‐engineering notation.

articles.title: Populism, radicalism, and protest mobilization by parties in Europe
articles.abstract: As European democracies struggle with a ‘crisis of representation’, populist parties appear to be instrumental in channeling popular discontent with governments across the continent, including through protests. While contemporary theories propose a strong connection between populism and protest mobilization, this has seldom been tested in a comparative perspective. At the same time, research has found that radical parties are more likely to mobilize for protests, and those parties are often also populist. We empirically disentangle these relationships with a comprehensive dataset of 4.8 million Facebook posts by all active sitting MPs in all EU27 national parliaments plus the UK between 2018 and 2023, using large language models to identify protest-related posts and those that announce protest events. Findings show that it is particularly radical parties mobilizing their followers, with populism itself having little additional explanatory power. This is the first cross-national, longitudinal evaluation of a much-touted theoretical connection between populist parties and protest mobilization, finding that it appears smaller and more conditional than prior research proposed.

articles.title: Federalism, Geography, and the Representation of Cities in the US Congress
articles.abstract: How elections impact the behavior of legislators is one of the most fundamental questions in the study of representation, yet little is known about the role of electoral geography. In a federal system like the United States, national resources often flow to cities. However, members of Congress represent congressional districts, which do not align with city boundaries. Using spending data from 1967 to 2019 and a within‐city research design, I show that the same city is represented differently depending on how it aligns with electoral maps. Cities benefit from having more representatives provided city residents still make up a substantial portion of each congressional district. These findings contribute to our understanding of representation within a federal system and illustrate how electoral geography can create inequalities in representation and the distribution of resources.

articles.title: Settler-Colonial Structure and Indigenous Agency
articles.abstract: Settler-colonial theory has become an influential framework in sociology. Yet its central claim—that settler-colonialism is an enduring structure organized by a “logic of elimination”—generates a theoretical paradox. If settler-colonialism is total, how can Indigenous agency be theorized without reproducing the structure it seeks to transcend? I address this tension by bringing sociological theories of structure and agency into dialogue with settler-colonial studies and Indigenous theory. Drawing on William Sewell Jr.’s conception of structure as the coupling of cultural schemas and material resources, I reinterpret two foundational concepts: the logic of elimination and the politics of recognition. Yet Indigenous theorists highlight forms of agency that exceed sociological accounts of action within a shared structural field. I therefore distinguish between interior agency, exercised within settler structures, and exterior agency, which sustains Indigenous worlds beyond them.

articles.title: Labour-market strategies and migration aspirations under legal uncertainty: Ukrainian refugees in Norway
articles.abstract: Drawing on twenty-three qualitative interviews, this study examines how labour-market strategies among highly educated Ukrainian refugees in Norway are shaped by migration aspirations under temporary protection. Existing research has largely treated labour-market integration and migration aspirations as separate phenomena, paying limited attention to how future aspirations influence refugees’ labour-market strategies. Building on theories of migration aspirations, social anchoring, and perceived opportunity structures, the analysis identifies three distinct labour-market strategies associated with different aspirations for settlement, return, and onward migration. The findings show that employment is understood as a means of securing legal stability, preserving professional identity, or developing resources for future mobility. Moreover, labour-market strategies are also shaped by how refugees perceive available opportunities through interactions with institutions, employers, and social networks. The article contributes to debates on refugee adaptation by showing how future orientations and perceived opportunity structures interact to shape labour-market navigation under conditions of legal uncertainty.

articles.title: Civil Servants and Democratic Backsliding: The Role of Managerial Signals
articles.authors: Mads Pieter van Luttervelt, Mathias Rask Østergaard-Nielsen, Martin Bækgaard, Zuzana Murdoch, Benny Geys
articles.abstract: Political efforts to weaken democratic institutions place civil servants in a dilemma between political responsiveness and protecting democratic values. As civil servants are embedded in the political-administrative hierarchy, we argue that signals from their direct hierarchical superiors are critical to understand how civil servants address this dilemma. Using a randomized survey experiment among Norwegian national-level civil servants (N = 1,446) and ordered logistic regression models, we find that democratic backsliding increases opposition to government wishes, internal and external voice, and consideration of exit from the organization. Managerial signals moderate these effects: civil servants are more inclined to voice concerns or consider exit when managers signal responsiveness to government wishes. In a conceptual replication and extension among US federal, state and local civil servants (N = 504) using ordered logistic regression models, we likewise find a greater inclination to exit if the manager signals responsiveness to government wishes, but also that respondents are less inclined to voice concerns to the manager. Overall, our findings imply that managerial signals within the political-administrative hierarchy are shaping civil servants’ immediate reactions to democratic backsliding.

articles.title: Beyond the Average: Revisiting How District Magnitude Shapes Party Systems
articles.abstract: We argue that district magnitude shapes the number of electoral parties through two mechanisms: district permissiveness, which influences incentives for electoral coordination within districts, and variation in district magnitude across districts within a country. When district magnitude varies within countries, larger districts tend to support a greater number of parties. Small parties that succeed in these districts are subsequently incentivized to compete in smaller districts, thereby weakening overall electoral coordination. Using cross-sectional data from 54 democracies and longitudinal evidence from 30 European countries between 1945 and 2019, we find that within-country variation in district magnitude increases the number of electoral parties in permissive electoral systems and erodes electoral coordination over time. We further examine the contamination mechanism from larger to smaller districts using district-level data from legislative elections in Portugal and Spain, both of which employ simple Proportional Representation systems with varying district magnitudes.

articles.authors: Daniel Casey, Thiago N. Silva, Pandanus Petter
articles.abstract: Question Time is a highly visible and adversarial parliamentary arena central to executive accountability, yet increasing personalisation may redirect scrutiny from collective party actors to individual leaders. This article analyses personalisation in Australian Question Time using more than 21,500 opposition questions asked between 1981 and 2025. We examine two dimensions of centralised personalisation: who asks opposition questions and whom those questions target, theorising variation through party structure (single-party vs coalition opposition) and institutional reforms to leadership selection rules. The findings challenge claims of a uniform rise in elite behavioural personalisation. While opposition questioning has become increasingly Prime Minister-centred over time, who asks questions follows a distinct pattern. Leader dominance varies across parties and institutional periods, rising in single-party oppositions but remaining lower and declining in coalitions, and falling further after leadership reforms. These results show that parliamentary personalisation is multi-dimensional and contingent on party organisation and institutional rules.

Different baselines, different outcomes: Reassessing the representative promise of within-party sortition
articles.abstract: Cowley, Webb and Bale’s critique of within-party sortition argues that lotteries among party members cannot produce a socially representative UK Parliament because party memberships are unrepresentative. Drawing on Party Members Project data, they show that random selection would produce only mixed improvements in descriptive representation. While their empirical contribution is significant, this article argues that the broader sceptical conclusion rests on a narrow modelling baseline. Cowley et al. effectively test only one institutional configuration—unstratified random selection from static party memberships—while extrapolating broader claims about sortition as a reform. This article develops three lines of critique. First, their simulations treat party membership as exogenous and unaffected by institutional change, ignoring evidence that candidate selection rules shape recruitment and participation. Second, their analysis evaluates only a single design variant, despite evidence that modern lottery-based institutions employ stratification and corrective mechanisms. Third, their evaluation relies on implicit ‘mirror of society’ standards without specifying formal metrics for aggregating representational trade-offs. Drawing on scholarship on sortition, deliberative democracy, and party organisation, the article proposes a dynamic and design-sensitive framework for evaluating within-party lotteries. Once alternative institutional baselines are considered, the representational potential of within-party sortition appears considerably less constrained than Cowley et al.’s analysis suggests.

Back to Feedback: Dynamics and Heterogeneity in Panel Data
articles.abstract: Many popular estimation methods in panel data rely on the assumption that the covariates of interest are strictly exogenous. However, this assumption is empirically restrictive in a wide range of settings. In this article I argue that credible empirical work requires meaningfully relaxing strict exogeneity assumptions. Econometricians have developed methods that allow for sequential exogeneity, which in contrast with strict exogeneity allows for the presence of feedback from past outcomes to future covariates or treatments. I review some of the classic work on linear models with constant coefficients, and then describe some approaches that allow for coefficient heterogeneity in models with feedback. Finally, in the last two parts of the article I review recent work that allows for sequential exogeneity in nonlinear panel data models, and mention possible extensions to network settings.

Behavioral profiling for compliance: the role of legitimacy, norms, and prior conduct
articles.authors: Michaela Assouline, Jonathan Slater, Yuval Feldman, Michael Gilead
articles.abstract: Understanding whether compliance tendencies generalize across legal domains is central to behavioral public policy. This study examines whether psychological mechanisms that shape compliance in one context also predict decisions in others. Using a multi-vignette survey conducted in the United Kingdom (N = 498) across 7 regulatory scenarios, we assess how perceptions of injunctive norms, reputational risk, attitudes toward legal objectives, legal legitimacy beliefs, perceived cost, perceived complexity, and self-efficacy influence stated compliance intentions. Several mechanisms show cross-domain consistency, although they are measured within each vignette. Legitimacy and injunctive norms are robust predictors, while moral costs and perceived risk exhibit moderate but patterned effects. Other influences, such as perceived burden or alignment with specific rules, vary more sharply across contexts, indicating that compliance reflects both situational features and cross-domain variation in interpretive tendencies. These findings have implications for trust-based and risk-based regulation. Cross-domain tendencies offer some support for differentiating oversight based on past behavior, yet the observed contextual variation cautions against mechanistic profiling. Effective regulatory design should combine broader psychological levers with context-specific strategies, recognizing both stability and flexibility in how people interpret legal demands. The study contributes to debates on the generalizability of compliance mechanisms and offers behavioral insights for more calibrated and responsive enforcement.

articles.title: Does alternative news media inform or misinform voters during election campaigns?
articles.authors: Atle Haugsgjerd, Rune Karlsen, Tine Figenschou, Karoline Andrea Ihlebæk, Toril Aalberg
articles.abstract: A growing body of literature has studied the audiences and effects of alternative media use. We contribute by examining how such usage shapes political knowledge during election campaigns. Given their partisan orientation, lack of professional verification, and often provocative style, alternative media are found to produce and circulate misinformation, even as their users are often politically engaged, active news consumers. We ask whether alternative media inform rather than misinform citizens during election campaigns. Adopting a two-dimensional conception of political knowledge, we examine both surveillance knowledge and confidence in that knowledge – along with misinformation understood as the combination of the two. Utilizing individual-level panel data from Norway, our findings suggest that alternative news use is not associated with being better or worse informed, but with being more confident in one’s political knowledge. We discuss how these effects may differ in more polarized or lower-quality information environments.

articles.title: Brand governance in the platform economy: From political to regulatory recognition
articles.abstract: This article reconceptualises corporate advocacy as brand governance, a techno-normative promotional practice that regulates the conditions of political visibility within networked publics. Drawing on a sociosemiotic analysis of global advocacy campaigns (2017–2022), the analysis identifies three strategies, Visionary (“Feeling the Other”), Sensitive (“Feeling for Others”) and Reflexive (“Feeling with Others”), each operating through distinct affective and narrative logics. The argument advances a distinction between political and regulatory recognition. Political recognition acknowledges claims in their structural and collective dimension; regulatory recognition extends legitimacy only to claims aligned with the promotional regime’s affective and reputational logic. The evidence suggests that brand governance operates predominantly in this regulatory mode, producing a conditional visibility that privileges individualised emotional appeals over structural political demands. This study focuses on US and Western European promotional cultures; comparative research across other regions remains a necessary next step.

articles.title: #BlackExcellence and #BlackGirlMagic are for all of us: Black influencers’ rejection of neoliberal logics and post-feminist discourses of entrepreneurship
articles.abstract: Situated within feminist media communication studies, this project uses critical technocultural discourse analysis to examine how #BlackExcellence emerges as a form of “digital Black practice” among Black women influencers and users. This study is framed within the context of the George Floyd protests in 2020 and 2021 as mainstream media outlets appropriated Black Excellence rhetoric in columns, listicles, and videos following this watershed moment. Analyses of popular press articles about Black influencers, discourse about race and labor on #BlackTumblr, influencer content on Instagram and YouTube, and interviews with Black influencers comprise the dataset. By leveraging intersectional platform affordances and racialized erotic capital, Black influencers subvert neoliberal and post-feminist logics undergirding digital labor by virtue of the racialized work they are expected to perform, challenging exceptionalist rhetoric. I argue that Black influencers’ uniquely racialized, gendered work contests the assumption that influencer labor is a natural outgrowth of neoliberal conditions.

articles.title: Audible, Spotify, YouTube & Co.: The German Digital Audiobook Market in the Context of Platformization
articles.abstract: This article examines the contemporary digital audiobook through the lens of platformization and develops a conceptual framework for understanding platformized audiobook culture. Drawing on an integrative review of interdisciplinary scholarship, supplemented by market reports, industry statistics, and audience studies, it uses the German audiobook market as an analytically illuminating example through which broader processes of platformization can be explored. The article situates audiobooks within wider transformations of everyday digital media practices, highlighting the shift from physical formats toward downloads and subscription-based streaming services. Conceptually, it distinguishes platformized audiobook culture from digital audiobook culture through two complementary analytical perspectives adapted from book studies, digital publishing, and media and communication studies: an integrative platform model and a data-environment model of streaming services. Building on this synthesis, the article proposes an ecosystem model of platformized audiobook culture to support future theoretical and empirical research.

articles.title: The intended and unintended affordances of post-separation parenting apps
articles.abstract: Little research has examined the role of specific technologies in relationships characterised by unequal power, such as those which underpin post-separation domestic and family violence. Drawing on the mechanisms and conditions framework of affordances and the methods of feature analysis, this study analyses 32 post-separation parenting apps along with in-depth interviews with 18 Australian victim–survivors who used these platforms with a perpetrator. We identify intended outcomes embedded in app design and contrast them with unintended outcomes emerging in practice. Analysis revealed that the design and promotional materials of the apps influence their use as a reinforcer of litigious mindsets and actions. This combination appears to change user behaviours, leading to communication becoming anticipatory and strategic with mixed outcomes.

articles.abstract: This study explores citizens’ attitudes towards European integration, moving beyond a simplistic ‘yes’ or ‘no’ perspective. Focusing on the EU–Swiss relationship, it examines a variety of integration questions using 2019 Swiss Election Study data. Latent profile analysis identifies five citizen groups that share similarities in support and opposition patterns regarding the studied questions: ‘pure sovereignists’, ‘neutrals’, ‘pure integrationists’, ‘cultural sovereignists’ and ‘economic integrationists’. The latter two groups are both comparatively more favourable of economic than cultural European integration, substantiating the claim that integration attitudes are multidimensional. Investigating the predictors of adherence to these two groups, the study finds education, income and party vote intentions to have a differentiated effect. Relevant group comparisons show that education and radical right vote intentions differentiate positions along the cultural, but not the economic, European integration dimension, whereas income, radical left and liberal vote intentions differentiate positions along the economic, but not the cultural, dimension.

articles.title: Innovative Finance for Urban Climate Action: From Financial Instruments to Governance Conditions
articles.authors: Pourya Salehi, Theo Kötter, Amy Jones, David Corbett, Jihyeon Jeong, Asad Asadzadeh
articles.abstract: Climate goals cannot be met without significant investment in cities, yet major gaps in climate finance, technical capacity, and access to capital markets persist. In response, a growing range of innovative finance methods have appeared. This article reviews the existing research on blended finance, green and sustainability-linked bonds, catastrophe and resilience bonds, land value capture, debt-for-nature swaps, and digital finance. The review finds that innovative finance should not be framed as a collection of instruments but as a governance framework that translates climate priorities into financial risk–return considerations, with effectiveness depending on supportive regulatory, fiscal, and institutional systems. Across instruments, financial innovation redistributes risk, aligns incentives, and reshapes public–private relationships. Effective strategies must therefore integrate instrument design with coordination, accountability, long-term value creation, and equitable climate outcomes across rapidly growing cities.

articles.title: Not Just Money or Jobs: How Family and Policy Shape Heterogeneous Configurations of Urban‐to‐Rural Talent Migration Decisions?
articles.authors: Hang Liu, Guosheng Deng, Bingling Wei
articles.abstract: Attracting and retaining skilled individuals remains a central challenge for rural development. This study examines how push, pull, and capability conditions combine to shape urban‐to‐rural talent migration decisions in China. Drawing on a survey of 1551 respondents across six provinces in eastern, central and western China, the study applies fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine the configurational effects of urban quality‐of‐life pressures, family care obligations, rural development prospects, PA, hometown attachment and self‐efficacy. The findings show that no single condition is necessary for an urban‐to‐rural migration decision. Instead, six sufficient configurations are grouped into four broader types: family‐care‐centred configurations, an external‐attraction configuration, a need‐fulfilment configuration and a capability‐enabled attraction configuration. Family care obligations and PA are prominent but configuration‐dependent conditions, whereas urban quality‐of‐life pressures operate primarily as a peripheral contextual condition. By integrating push, pull and capability perspectives within a configurational framework, this study advances a talent‐centred account of counter‐urbanisation. The findings suggest that rural talent policies should move beyond uniform incentives and address heterogeneous combinations of family needs, perceived opportunities, place‐based ties and individual capabilities.

articles.title: Boomerang Young Adults in Seoul, South Korea: Residential Pathways, Health and Social Attitudes
articles.abstract: Leaving the parental home is a key transition to adulthood. However, recent sociodemographic changes have produced more diverse residential pathways such as delayed home‐leaving or returning to the parental home (‘boomerang movers’). While prior research has focused on the characteristics and determinants of these patterns, few studies have examined how various residential pathways are related to trajectories of health and social attitudes in Korea. We used longitudinal data from the annual Seoul Young Adult Panel Study (2021–2024) of individuals aged 18–34 interviewed ≥ 2 waves ( n = 4895) and identified 4 residential pathways: persistent coresidence, persistent independence, boomerang and transition into independence. Outcomes were self‐rated health, suicidal ideation, social outlook (expectations regarding Korea's future relative to the present) and perceived social fairness. Mixed‐effects models were then estimated to examine differences in levels and rates across pathways. Compared with persistent coresidence, persistent independence was associated with a lower probability of reporting suicidal ideation at baseline and slower decreases over time. Boomerang adults had lower self‐rated health and higher suicidal ideation at baseline. However, they showed greater improvements over time: faster gains in self‐rated health, a more rapid decline in the likelihood of reporting suicidal ideation, larger increases in perceived social fairness and a less pronounced decline in social outlook. No significant differences were observed for the transition into independence group. Overall, residential pathways are linked to distinct trajectories of health and social attitudes during emerging adulthood. Boomerang living reflects initial disadvantages, gradual improvements and adaptation among urban young adults.

articles.title: Crossing Boundaries in Myanmar: Strategies of Boundary‐Making vis‐à‐vis Nativist Citizenship Imaginary
articles.abstract: This article examines popular narratives in Myanmar that use physical characteristics, such as skin colour, to argue that certain minority groups are non‐native and originally from the Indian subcontinent, and how effectively the military junta has enforced this view. Using Andreas Wimmer's (2013) typology of boundary‐making strategies, this research examines the experiences of unofficial Muslim minorities in the townships of Mingala Taungnyunt and Tamwe, Yangon, before the 2021 military coup, as well as early coup accounts, to discuss alleged discriminatory rhetoric by the Burmese State in determining who qualifies as part of the population it governs. The analysis is situated within the Citizenship Law of 1982, which created distinct categories of citizenship, and the supposedly privileged position of the Bamar people within the official list of 135 national races, tracing incentives for both closure and strategic inclusion. A first‐glance examination of discourses from above may suggest that physical traits are used to restrict access to resources and affirm group identities, with extreme categorisation increasing reliance on markers of distinction. Yet a deeper analysis from below reveals that association and discrimination extend beyond racial or ethnic prejudice, with many individuals unaware of their friends' and relatives' ethnic backgrounds. I argue that this apparent contradiction reflects not inconsistent enforcement, but strategic ambiguity: the state's classificatory apparatus is intentionally loose, and this looseness leaves room for individuals to negotiate, contest and reshape the boundaries it imposes. This research demonstrates how individuals engage with, challenge and reshape these processes, even as local governments manipulate citizenship membership.

articles.title: Healing at Home or Re‐Marginalisation? Perceived Neighbourhood Environment, Sense of Belonging and Mental Health of Return Migrants in Peri‐Urban China
articles.abstract: Amidst China's transition into a new phase of urbanisation, the mental health of return migrants has emerged as a critical issue. Whether returning to rural communities offers the spiritual solace of ‘healing at home’ or precipitates a descent into ‘re‐marginalisation’ remains poorly understood, particularly in metropolitan peri‐urban villages where remembered hometowns are being reshaped by urbanisation. Drawing on the survey of return migrants in peri‐urban Zhengzhou, this study constructs and validates a moderated mediation model based on field survey data to systematically investigate the mechanisms underlying the impact of neighbourhood environmental perception on the mental health of returnees. The findings reveal that: (1) more favourable perceptions of both built and social neighbourhood environments were associated with fewer mental health problems, and perceived built environment was positively associated with perceived social environment; (2) multi‐scalar sense of belonging played a mediating role in the associations between perceived neighbourhood environments and mental health, with village belonging representing the more prominent mediating pathway and highlighting the role of emotional identification in return migrants' post‐return adaptation; and (3) migration experience moderated the association between village belonging and mental health: longer out‐migration duration attenuated the protective association of village belonging with mental health, whereas a higher host‐city tier and greater perceived social exclusion strengthened its negative association with mental health problems. This study uncovers the spatial‐emotional interactive mechanisms of psychological adaptation among return migrants, providing a robust theoretical basis and practical pathways for enhancing the mental health of returnee populations through the improvement of human settlements and community governance.
