articles.title: Checks, Balances, and Presidential Ambitions
articles.authors: Christian Fong, Kenneth Lowande, Ayse Eldes
articles.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between running for president and members’ contributions to the core legislative functions that impact Congress’s standing relative to the presidency. This study finds some evidence that ambitious legislators attend roll call votes and oversight hearings at lower rates, but at the same time, they are more legislatively productive, conduct just as much informal oversight and are equally informational in their public oversight. When Congress votes on an issue that affects the balance of power between Congress and the president, they are more likely to side with Congress than legislators without presidential ambitions are. These behavioral differences persist even after their presidential runs, which suggests they are not driven by a strategic effort to audition for the presidency.

articles.title: Social learning behind closed doors: evidence from seniority voting in the US Supreme Court
articles.abstract: We analyze the implications of seniority voting on Supreme Court decision-making. We provide reduced-form evidence consistent with justices learning from the votes of their senior colleagues as determined by the voting mechanism. To explain this evidence, we develop and estimate a model of sequential voting with social learning. In the model, justices weigh spatial payoffs against the appropriateness of their disposition and consider their preferences, private information and the choices of senior justices. We recover estimates of judicial preferences, expertise and learning and use them to assess the quality of Supreme Court dispositions relative to alternative voting mechanisms. We find that the quality of the Court’s dispositions would have improved under an anti-seniority rule, in which junior justices are allowed to vote first.

articles.title: The institutional politics of development finance: ODA’s role in shaping subnational DFI investments
articles.authors: Nicolas Bau, Simone Dietrich, Jing Qian, Duy Trinh
articles.abstract: Development finance institutions (DFIs), operated by donor governments to support private sector development in the Global South, often face informational barriers when deciding where to invest abroad. We argue that traditional Official Development Assistance (ODA), delivered through bilateral aid agencies, can guide these investment decisions. Specifically, aid agencies generate valuable, location-specific, investment-relevant knowledge through their ODA-funded activities across regions of the Global South. When shared with DFIs, this information reduces uncertainty and increases the likelihood of DFI investment in those same regions. To test this expectation, we leverage an original geocoded dataset comprising investments by 12 DFIs from 12 OECD-DAC donor countries, matched with subnational ODA data from the GODAD dataset for the period 2000–2020. Our quantitative analyses reveal a robust and consistent association between ODA activity and DFI entry at the subnational level. To probe the mechanism, we conduct qualitative case studies of Germany, France, and the United States, illustrating how aid agencies and DFIs exchange information and coordinate investment decisions. Our findings contribute to a growing literature on the spatial allocation of development finance and provide new insight into how traditional ODA and national DFIs interact as part of an evolving development cooperation bureaucracy.

articles.title: Contesting Norms and Challenging Order: Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023 and the Geopolitics of LGBTIQ+ Human Rights
articles.abstract: Uganda’s adoption of the Anti-Homosexuality Act in 2023 reveals significant contestation among domestic and external actors regarding LGBTIQ+ human rights norms. This article argues that opposition to LGBTIQ+ rights has become central to contemporary challenges to the liberal international order by contesting the authority of liberal human rights norms as universal benchmarks of state legitimacy. Drawing on critical IR theories of norm violation, it analyzes how external actors responded to the Act and how Ugandan state actors defended the legislation. The article concludes that political opposition against LGBTIQ+ human rights in Uganda, akin to anti-LGBTIQ+ politics observed elsewhere in the world, has become central to political critique of “the West” and the existing international order.

articles.title: Law and Political Violence against Women in Central America
articles.abstract: Cristiana Chamorro Barrios is a Nicaraguan journalist and founder of the Nicaraguan Foundation for Freedom of the Press, a nonprofit focused on promoting freedom of expression and public access to information, as well as providing training and support to local journalists. Cristiana was arrested on June 2, 2021, in Managua, Nicaragua, on accusations of tax evasion (International Society for Human Rights 2025). At the time of her arrest, Cristiana, a member of a prominent Nicaraguan family, had recently announced her intention to challenge Daniel Ortega in the November 2021 presidential election and was widely considered the favorite in the race. The charges against Cristiana 1 — including the vague claim of “abusive management and ideological falsehood” — though made with no evidence, disqualified her from running for office. She was later tried in sham proceedings and sentenced to eight years in prison. In 2023, Cristiana was one of hundreds of political prisoners forcibly expelled from the country and later stripped of their citizenship (Abi-Habib 2023; Confidencial 2021). 2

articles.title: Civil Servants' Compliance with Conflict‐of‐Interest Regulation: Evidence from a List Experiment
articles.authors: Don S. Lee, Minsung Michael Kang, Soonae Park
articles.abstract: While regulatory governance scholarship has paid significant attention to the normative importance of ethics reform in government, empirical evidence on compliance remains scant. Drawing on insights from the social value activation model and behavioral ethics, this study examines civil servants' compliance propensity under conflict‐of‐interest regulation. Specifically, we examine how a legitimate ethics reform is associated with the voluntary compliance of two legally treated groups: those with policy implementation duties and those with frequent stakeholder engagement. The results of our list experiment with a representative sample of South Korean civil servants ( n = 1977) show that both target groups exhibit higher estimated compliance propensity with the second provision of the Act, restricted and prohibited actions, but that only policy implementation duties are associated with higher compliance propensity with the first provision, reporting and disclosure obligations. Our findings suggest that ethics reform compliance is shaped not only by formal rules and deterrence, but also by administrative role exposure, perceived legitimacy, and the value‐based dimension of civil servants.

articles.title: The Rational Design of Space Agreements: How Bilateralism Shapes Powerful States' Design Preferences
articles.authors: Jean‐Frédéric Morin, Philippe Evoy, Cynthia Couette
articles.abstract: The global governance of outer space relies heavily on international agreements, yet the institutional forms of these agreements remain underexplored. This article introduces a new dataset on various design features of 952 space agreements, offering the first large‐N overview of institutional design in space governance. Building on rational design theory, this article analyzes how these design features interact with one another and with negotiation structures. Our results reveal systematic trade‐offs and suggest that power asymmetry has contrasting effects depending on the context: Powerful states tend to favor greater delegation, precision, and enforcement in bilateral agreements, while often resisting them in multilateral settings. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for both power dynamics and bilateralism, two contextual factors often overlooked in rational design theory. By making the dataset publicly available, the article seeks to foster further research on the causes and consequences of institutional variation in space governance and to advance comparative institutionalist scholarship across issue‐areas of global governance.

articles.title: Legal Corruption in the Government: An Experimental Study on the Role of Civil Servants' Political Ideology
articles.authors: Kee Hoon Chung, Don S. Lee, Soonae Park
articles.abstract: Legal corruption, also known as institutional corruption, has become prevalent in the public sector, but empirical research on this subject is still at a nascent stage. Given its potentially detrimental impact on the perceived level of organizational capacity among internal members, understanding civil servants' views of legal corruption is essential. We contribute to this literature a discussion of civil servants' assessment of legal corruption in the government and evidence from a survey experiment with more than 2000 South Korean civil servants. The results of our analysis suggest that civil servants evaluate the degree of legal corruption in the government through their political lens, that is, their political ideology. Specifically, they tend to be more critical when the government is ruled by a chief executive and party that have different political views from their own, compared to when it is governed by those with the same political views. The implications of this study are clear: the central role of political views and policy preferences in understanding perceptions of legal corruption in the public sector.

articles.title: Legislative Financial Asset Disclosure, Firm Motivations, and Macroeconomic Outcomes in the US States
articles.authors: Justin H. Kirkland, Patrick E. Shea
articles.abstract: Financial asset disclosure laws are widely implemented to combat conflicts of interest among policymakers, yet their economic impact remains poorly understood. This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of how these transparency measures affect macroeconomic outcomes across the 50 US states. We theorize that these disclosure and recusal laws could have divergent impacts on macroeconomic performance: they might enhance economic outcomes by curtailing the exploitation of political connections by business firms, or conversely, they could impede economic growth by altering firm behavior and deterring business leaders from seeking public office, thereby potentially reducing the pool of economically savvy policymakers. Using new data on state‐level disclosure policies, we find that asset disclosure laws are associated with a worsening macroeconomic environment in states. To uncover the mechanisms driving these counterintuitive results, we conduct two pre‐registered survey experiments with 2000 small business owners. Our experimental evidence suggests that stringent disclosure requirements deter business investment and expansion. This research has implications for legislative challenges for legislative design, transparency, and economic policy.

articles.title: Policy Window as a Trapdoor: Rethinking the Multiple Streams Framework through the Defunding of U.S. Public Media
articles.authors: Hilde Van den Bulck, Christopher Ali, Jonathan Kropko
articles.abstract: This article analyses the 2025 defunding of U.S. public media as a critical case to revisit Kingdon’s multiple streams framework (MSF). While MSF offers a useful heuristic for understanding policy change through the convergence of problem, policy, and political streams, its explanatory power is limited by assumptions of contingency, pluralism, and stakeholder inclusion. Under growing illiberalism, the “policy window” functioned less as an accidental opening than as a trapdoor, built through ideological persistence, institutional erosion and coordinated policy design. Drawing on critical discourse analysis of congressional hearings, executive orders, political communication, and media coverage, alongside survey data on public broadcasting system audiences, this study shows how conservative actors sustained a politicized definition of public media bias and institutionalized policy solutions. The survey highlights a disjuncture between audience trust and the construction of public media as a policy problem. Rather than spontaneous convergence, the case reflects coordinated restructuring of the public media system. More broadly, it suggests that MSF becomes less effective when stream independence is undermined by executive dominance and ideological alignment, requiring approaches that foreground power, discourse, and exclusion.

articles.title: An Effort Made for Whom? Exploring Ministers’ Public Approval and Name Recognition in Relation to Their Media Activity
articles.authors: Mads Fuglsang Hove, Jonas Krogh Madsen, Peter Heyn Nielsen
articles.abstract: In many democracies, cabinet ministers find themselves in a difficult situation, juggling a demanding administrative job with political responsibilities and the need to communicate and campaign to secure reelection. With the rise of social media, this balance is becoming increasingly unstable. However, the tangible benefits of media visibility outside election campaigns remain unclear, making it difficult to determine whether such efforts yield meaningful political returns. This study examines and compares whether Danish ministers’ media activities—both in traditional and social media—impact their name recognition and popularity in the Danish population. We utilize thirty-two nationally representative opinion polls conducted between March 2020 and May 2024 and merge these with extensive records of all Danish ministers’ Facebook activity and appearances in traditional media outlets throughout the same period. Overall, our findings show that ministers’ activity in traditional media is associated with only minor gains in name recognition, while social media activity has either zero or minimal gains in popularity. Moreover, breaking down these correlations across different types of Facebook interactions and traditional media outlets suggests a trade-off between reaching and being perceived favorably by voters, showing the multifaceted nature of (social) media activity. Consequently, while we do not rule out any significant effects of social media on voters’ perceptions, we argue that social media activity is no panacea for politicians to improve their public popularity and name recognition.

articles.title: Incivility Among Politicians: Driven by Rational Minds or Personal Drives?
articles.abstract: There is growing concern about politicians engaging in incivility by mocking and insulting each other. While prior research often explains such discourse through rational choice, emerging work highlights the role of politicians’ individual traits, such as their personality. Yet, a unified theoretical account of how rationality and individual predispositions interact to shape harmful elite discourse is lacking. Drawing on foundational insights from psychology, we argue that politicians’ discourse reflects primarily rational considerations, which are moderated by their individual predispositions, leading to uncivil communication between politicians. We test this notion using elite survey data, unobtrusive measures of their individual traits, and direct observations of politicians’ social media communication in Belgium – a rare integration of psychological and behavioral evidence at the elite level. The results show that politicians’ use of uncivil discourse responds to rational considerations, but that the strength of this response depends on their individual predispositions. These findings demonstrate that individual traits moderate how politicians translate rational incentives into harmful discourse, providing a more nuanced account of the causes of elite incivility.

articles.title: Narratives of Power: AI, Agency and the EU AI Act
articles.abstract: Public debate around AI has been characterised by hegemonic narratives that delineate the scope of the conversation, suppressing different voices and limiting nuanced discussion of the technology’s harms and benefits. Scholars have identified technological or enchanted determinism, the arms race mentality and the utopia versus dystopia debate as key narratives around AI. These ideas saturate the conversation, driven primarily by the tech industry, which positions itself as the (only) expert voice. The industry’s capacity to drive these narratives is facilitated by its established institutional authority and dominant presence in public discourse, as well as the knowledge asymmetry inherent in the proprietary, ‘black-box’ nature of AI systems. Tech firms leverage the technical opacity of AI and their powerful societal position to define the contours of public debate, assigning agency to AI itself and the tech industry; constructing users and civil society as passive observers or recipients; and establishing a frame for debate that focuses on extreme consequences or hyperbolic benefits. This study, conducted early in 2024, investigates the effects of this interpretive frame on the policy choices and communications of the EU AI Act, through a mixed-methods computational and critical discourse analysis. Within EU governing body texts, the same discursive patterns that map agency and erase the middle ground of debate in AI are found, helping to marginalise alternative perspectives from other stakeholders and prevent nuanced understandings of potential harms. In the context of the Act itself, these patterns reverberate in the assignment of agentic roles and the scope of the regulation.

articles.title: Agrivoltaics can reduce political polarization and local opposition to solar energy on land
articles.authors: Lukas Fesenfeld, Leon Sistek, Simon Montfort, Dionis Anderegg, Jürg Rohrer, Tobias Schmidt
articles.abstract: As solar energy deployment on land intensifies, political polarization and local opposition increasingly challenge its social acceptance. We propose that agrivoltaics – a dual land-use technology that combines solar power generation with agricultural production – can help bridge ideological divides and reduce local opposition by minimizing land-use conflicts and offering additional benefits to rural communities. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a pre-registered, field-embedded experiment with a representative sample (2145 Swiss residents) just prior to a national renewable energy referendum, combining a personalized geolocated information treatment on local agrivoltaics potential with a conjoint experiment varying key technology and project design attributes. Here we show that agrivoltaics garners broad public support across ideological groups and reduces local opposition, especially when projects are well integrated into agricultural landscapes, do not significantly reduce agricultural yields, and are locally owned. These findings underscore the importance of technology and project design in addressing local and right-leaning opposition to land-based solar energy.

articles.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) significantly contributes to the mental health burden in Africa, requiring insights into prevalence and risk factors to inform culturally responsive care. This study assessed current and lifetime MDD prevalence and associated factors among 7,073 adults from hospital settings in Uganda, Kenya, Ethiopia, and South Africa within the NeuroGAP-Psychosis study. Prevalence was 0.9% for current MDD and 5.1% for lifetime MDD, substantially lower than prior estimates from the region. Lower rates may be due to the population studied or cultural variations in expression of symptoms. Multilevel logistic regression identified significant associations between current MDD and negative life events, alcohol use, and Kessler psychological distress scores, while lifetime MDD was linked to age, female sex, chronic pain, frequent headaches, and positive psychosis screening. These findings underscore the need for targeted mental health interventions tailored to the identified factors to reduce the burden of MDD in diverse African contexts.

articles.title: Dynamic population presence linked to home neighbourhoods in the Helsinki Metropolitan Area: A 24-hour weekday and weekend dataset
articles.authors: Kerli Müürisepp, Olle Järv, Matti Manninen, Tuuli Toivonen
articles.abstract: In this article, we present a 24-hour population presence dataset from the Helsinki Metropolitan Area (HMA), Finland. This population-level and metropolitan-wide dataset shows hourly population distribution across HMA neighbourhoods on an average weekday (Mon–Fri) and an average weekend day (Sat–Sun), and links people’s hourly presence to their home neighbourhoods. The dataset was derived from mobile phone data, collected by a major Finnish mobile network operator in 2021, through anonymisation, spatio-temporal aggregation, normalisation, and weighting based on neighbourhood population data from Statistics Finland. The published data serve as a calibrated and validated proxy for the entire HMA population distribution. Data validation showed strong agreement between the population register data and the study population’s residential and night-time presence distribution. By linking dynamic presence data to home neighbourhoods, the dataset allows both people-based and place-based analyses, and integration with socioeconomic indicators. Moreover, its population-level scope, metropolitan-wide coverage, and capture of both weekdays and weekends makes the dataset valuable for a range of research questions and policy applications related to daily mobility, urban vitality, social mixing, green space use, epidemic modelling, and beyond.

articles.title: Romantic love related relationships picture dataset (Love_Pic Dataset)
articles.authors: Yudie Zhang, Shuqin Liu, Min Shao, Lu Chen, Huiling Qian, Zilong Wei, Wenbo Peng, Jing Meng
articles.abstract: Current picture datasets lack sufficient materials to investigate complex romantic love relationships (falling in love, being single, break-up). Addressing this gap, we developed the Romantic Love Related Relationships Picture Dataset (Love_Pic Dataset), comprising 26 love, 22 single, and 23 break-up pictures. These pictures underwent rigorous validation for relationship identification, affective valence, and arousal level by 114 participants (57 females). Results confirmed distinct emotional profiles: Love pictures elicited the most positive affective valences and highest arousal levels. Single pictures evoked moderate affective valences and moderate arousal levels. Break-up pictures induced the most negative affective valences, though with moderate arousal levels. The Love_Pic Dataset demonstrates strong internal consistency, confirming its reliability. This validated resource provides an essential tool for future research exploring the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying romantic love relationships. Furthermore, it enables investigation into bystanders’ emotional reactions to depictions of these relationship states. The Love_Pic Dataset is openly available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BNVJQ .

articles.title: “Fairness Labels” in Feeds: Process Disclosures, Provenance, and User Choice Among Short‑Video Creators in Mainland China
articles.abstract: Algorithmically ranked feeds allocate attention in ways that can reproduce inequalities in visibility. We test whether a compact, feed-level process disclosure —a banner describing exposure-safeguard governance, paired with provenance cues and in-situ user-choice affordances—improves perceived procedural justice, distributive fairness, and legitimacy among short-video creators in mainland China. In a mobile-first online experiment with 1,154 research-verified PRC creators in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), participants viewed a realistic feed randomized to No label , Personalization notice , or Fairness disclosure ; within the fairness condition, we factorially varied frame (Safeguards/Parity/Quotas/Exposure-fairness), issuer provenance (platform vs. independent audit), and disclosure depth (minimal badge vs. brief rationale). The compound fairness disclosure increased perceived procedural justice, distributive fairness, and legitimacy relative to both controls and was accompanied by lower self-censorship and higher voice intentions. Effects were directionally stronger in civic/news contexts and among creators who self-identified as marginalized or previously down-ranked. Within-arm exploratory diagnostics suggested that quota-like parity framing may yield directionally lower legitimacy than exposure-fairness framing, while audit cues produced directionally positive but imprecise trust gains. Backfire checks found no implied-unfairness spillover for unlabeled items and no interaction with per-item AI-content labels, although AI labels reduced perceived accuracy. Together, these findings suggest that governance-aligned micro-disclosures can function as procedural visibility signals for creators, while underscoring the importance of verifiable claims and careful disclosure design.

articles.title: Sharing the Alternative – The Role of Digital Platforms for Alternative News-Sharing Behavior
articles.abstract: In a time of growing concerns over factual accuracy in the public sphere, alternative news media have emerged as a counterpoint to traditional mass media. In Germany, many online-only outlets cater to a rising audience, driven by distinct goals, standards, and funding structures compared to what they term ‘elite media’. Digital platforms are vital to their success, enabling audience growth with minimal financial investment and bypassing legacy media systems’ critique and verification mechanisms. Their reach, however, relies on followers sharing content and leveraging social media’s network effect to amplify niche information. Yet, the sharing habits of alternative news audiences remain understudied. This study uses original survey data from over 2,000 German alternative news users (collected in September 2023), exploring whether these patterns drive alternative media’s rise as a counterweight to established journalism. We investigate users’ sharing activity, their motivations for sharing news or refraining from it, and sociodemographic/ideological predictors for alternative news sharing.

articles.title: Right-Wing Shift? Evaluating Authoritarianism, Social Dominance, and System Justification Among People of Color Before and After the 2024 Election
articles.authors: Emily Ortiz, Ramona Alhambra, Andrew M. Engelhardt, Efrén Pérez
articles.abstract: Non-trivial shares of people of color (PoC) have long identified as Republicans, and many of them helped cement Donald Trump’s 2024 re-election. How durable was this shift toward the political right among some PoC? We test two claims in this brief research note. First, consistent with polarization literature, we claim that partisanship primed three conservative postures among Republican PoC during the 2024 campaign: authoritarianism, social dominance orientation, and system justification. Second, aligning with work on expressive survey responses, we argue that these postures faded significantly once Trump’s agenda produced visibly harmful consequences for PoC (e.g., deportation raids; weakened civil rights). Leveraging a three-wave panel of Black, Latino, and Asian adults ( N = 3,626), our pre-registered analyses indicate Republican partisanship in June 2024 heightened authoritarianism, social dominance, and system justification among Black, Latino, and Asian adults in December 2024. These patterns were fleeting, with partisanship’s impact on these postures withering by July 2025. We find scattered evidence that these postures intensified PoC’s Republican partisanship during this period, implying our results reflect campaign effects rather than an unerring endorsement of these right-wing inclinations among Republican PoC.

articles.title: Prime Locations
articles.authors: Gabriel M. Ahlfeldt, Thilo N. H. Albers, Kristian Behrens
articles.abstract: We develop a method for delineating prime locations—ultradense clusters of economic activity—within cities and apply it to comprehensive establishment data covering all US metropolitan areas. We further use big data to extend the analysis to a global context where administrative data are sparse. Many cities in the United States and around the world are dominated by a small number of prime locations that can concentrate up to one-half of tradable services jobs on tiny shares of land and are dominant centers of economic gravity. In cities with fewer prime locations, a larger tradable services share concentrates in them. (JEL C55, R23, R32, R38, R52, R58)

articles.title: What Is Newsworthy? Theory and Evidence
articles.authors: Luis Armona, Matthew Gentzkow, Emir Kamenica, Jesse M. Shapiro
articles.abstract: We introduce a model in which a benevolent news outlet decides whether to report the realization of a state to a consumer, who pays a cost to receive it. A simple statistical rule, called a proper scoring rule, describes when the outlet should be more likely to report the realization. Using data from the US television news, we show that a particular scoring rule successfully predicts many salient features of news reporting. We show how to use this rule as a control variable to discipline tests of reporting bias, and we show that controlling for it matters in our applications. (JEL D83, C44, L82)

articles.title: Pricing with Algorithms
articles.abstract: This paper studies Markov perfect equilibria in a repeated duopoly model where sellers choose algorithms. An algorithm is a mapping from the competitor's price to own price. Once set, the algorithms respond quickly. Customers arrive randomly, and sellers can periodically revise their algorithms. The main results are that (i) for the simple two-price model with standard profit functions, monopoly pricing is the unique equilibrium outcome and (ii) for any general finite price grid, all equilibrium outcomes feature supracompetitive pricing. Sustenance of such collusion seems outside the scope of current antitrust laws, for it does not involve any direct communication. (JEL C73, D21, D43, K21)

articles.title: Unconditional Convergence in Manufacturing: A Reassessment
articles.authors: Berthold Herrendorf, Richard Rogerson, Ákos Valentinyi
articles.abstract: The movement of labor out of agriculture is a central feature of the development process. A long-held view is that successful development requires that much of the labor released from agriculture be allocated to manufacturing rather than services. Rodrik's (2013) finding of unconditional convergence for manufacturing productivity, using data from UNIDO, provided empirical support for this view. We argue that the UNIDO data are ill-suited for studying cross-country productivity dynamics. Using recently released GGDC data designed for this purpose, we revisit the issue and find no evidence of unconditional convergence in manufacturing productivity over 1990–2018. (JEL D24, J24, L60, O13, O14, O47, Q10)

articles.title: The Missing Middle Managers: Labor Costs, Firm Structure, and Development
articles.authors: Jonas Hjort, Hannes Malmberg, Todd Schoellman
articles.abstract: Using data obtained from human resources consulting firms, we document the cost to large firms of hiring managers and business professionals in 146 countries worldwide. The average pay in the poorest decile of countries is $18,000 per year, which is 9.7 times GDP per worker. In contrast, in the richest decile of countries, large firms pay managers and business professionals only 0.8 times GDP per worker. We use an appropriate technology model to show that the cost of management could be an important deterrent to the expansion of the modern sector in developing countries. (JEL J23, J24, J31, L84, M10, M51, O15)

articles.title: The Missing Loan-to-Value Cycle
articles.authors: Manuel Adelino, W. Ben McCartney, Antoinette Schoar
articles.abstract: We show that the equilibrium loan-to-value (LTV) distribution in the US mortgage market has been remarkably stable over the last quarter century, both in aggregate and region by region, despite large, cross-sectionally heterogeneous house price cycles. While high-LTV mortgages changed from being explicitly government backed to privately securitized and back, their overall fraction remained unchanged. A repeat-sales methodology and an analysis of loan performance confirm that this stability in the distribution of LTVs holds even within subgroups of the population. These findings are inconsistent with models of credit cycles that use changes in collateral constraints to generate boom-and-bust dynamics in house prices. (JEL C43, E32, G21, G51, R21, R31)

articles.title: How Test-Optional Policies in College Admissions Disproportionately Harm High-Achieving Applicants from Disadvantaged Backgrounds
articles.authors: Bruce Sacerdote, Douglas O. Staiger, Michele Tine
articles.abstract: We analyze data from one elite institution and find that test score–optional policies harm the likelihood of admission for high-achieving applicants from disadvantaged backgrounds. Under test-optional policies, these applicants submit test scores at too low a rate; they more than double their admission probability (from 2.9 percent to 7.2 percent) by reporting scores. Our findings suggest that, more than commonly understood, elite institutions interpret test scores in the context of an applicant's background. Thus, availability of test scores on an application can promote rather than hinder social mobility. (JEL I23, I28)

articles.title: Screening Adaptive Cartels
articles.authors: Juan Ortner, Sylvain Chassang, Kei Kawai
articles.abstract: We propose an equilibrium theory of data-driven antitrust oversight in which regulators launch investigations on the basis of suspicious bidding patterns and cartels can adapt to the statistical screens used by regulators. Our main result establishes that screening for collusion using tests with a low false-positive rate (safe tests) is a robust improvement over laissez-faire. Safe tests do not create new collusive equilibria and do not hurt competitive industries. In addition, safe tests can have strict bite, including unraveling all collusive equilibria in some settings. (JEL D21, D43, D44, K21, L12, L14)

articles.title: Auditing urban nature access claims for sustainable city governance
articles.abstract: Urban governments use nature-access indicators to assess biodiversity, health, equity and regenerative-planning goals, yet policy conclusions can depend on how the claim is constructed. We audit six specifications—inventory, access geometry, distance model, threshold, population allocation and vulnerability definition—using three purposive core cities, transfer checks, a 30-city data-readiness screen and an entrance-aware London validation. Plausible alternatives changed access levels by up to 48.82 percentage points, reversed some environmental-justice classifications and substantially altered underserved target populations. A matched London diagnostic showed that network penalties narrowed from 36.95 points at 300 m to 0.52 points at 1000 m. We therefore propose a decision-stability envelope that reports a preferred specification alongside ranges, equity-direction changes, target-set reclassification and missing operational data. The cases are not globally representative; they demonstrate an auditable workflow for testing whether urban nature claims are sufficiently stable to guide regenerative and equitable planning.
